title: Atterbeary goes on the air, GOP goes on the attack, more in political notes
summary: Former Del. Vanessa Atterbeary goes on the air with TV ads in the Howard County Executive race, House Republicans are still steamed about the Sine Die shouting match and Comptroller Brooke Lierman has a new chief of staff, in political notes.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters April 24, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters April 24, 2026

With two months to go before the primary, former Del. Vanessa Atterbeary (D-Howard) hit the airwaves on Thursday with her first television ad in the Howard County executive race.

Atterbeary, who served for more than a decade in the General Assembly, touted her record opposing book bans, and supporting gun control measures. She cast herself as a county executive who would oppose the policies of President Donald Trump (R).

“Trump’s fascist agenda is threatening our rights, our federal workers and our future,” she said in the ad.

Atterbeary faces a crowded Democratic field in the primary June 23, that includes two Howard County Council members and small businessman Bob Cockey. The race will be won in the primary, because there is no Republican candidate in the ring to replace the term-limited executive, Calvin Ball (D).

A poll released by Council Member Liz Walsh’s campaign earlier this month showed Atterbeary with the lead, at 17% of the vote, while Walsh had 13% and Council Member Deb Jung had 12%. But it indicated that a significant percentage of voters, 58%, are undecided.

“This is a wide open race with a strong path to victory for Liz Walsh,” read a statement from Walsh’s campaign manager Sean Ford.

After pollsters at Hart Research provided a statement about the background of each candidate, Walsh took the lead according to her campaign, receiving 33% of the vote to Atterbeary’s 29% and Jung’s 16%.

“We did a poll a few weeks ago, and I’m flattered that my poll and apparently her poll showed me winning right now,” Atterbeary said in an interview on Thursday. “But I’m running like I’m 10 points behind. I’m not taking anything for granted.”

The televised ad, which will appear to Howard County viewers watching channels such as CNN and MS NOW, is part of a six-figure ad buy. The campaign also plans to run additional advertisements in the future, Atterbeary said. Atterbeary is the only candidate in the race not using public financing, and has taken the lead on fundraising.

Atterbeary said her goal with the ad was to show off her experience taking on “tough fights” in the state legislature, including against the National Rifle Association and Moms for Liberty.

“I stood up to them, and I plan to do the same thing here in Howard County as executive, so that was definitely an inspiration for the ad,” Atterbeary said.

The ad focuses on Atterbeary’s goals to improve the education system, and features children prominently — including her own son and daughter, who were delighted to be on TV.

“We are very excited about the ad — my kids are very excited,” Atterbeary said.

House Republicans were still steaming days later about the last-minute blowup on the floor of the House on Sine Die, when members on both sides of the aisle were up on their feet and hollering at each other as leadership pushed through final vote on the Maryland Voting Rights Act of 2026.

The measure had been debated for close to an hour, but as the clock ticked toward midnight Del. Dana Stein (D-Baltimore County) called the question — an undebatable motion that moves an issue straight to vote. Republicans, seizing their last chance to stop the bill, rose to explain their votes, but Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) refused to recognize them and called the vote.

The storm after the calm: Placid final day erupts in final minutes in House, Senate

In a three-page letter to Peña-Melnyk last Friday, House Minority Leader Jason Buckel (R-Allegany) said the refusal to recognize members to explain their votes not only violated decorum, it also violated House rules. Under Rule 94, he said, members are guaranteed the right to explain their votes, and under Rule 12 they are allowed to challenge a ruling of the chair — which Buckel did, but Peña-Melnyk ignored.

“In my 12 years in the House of Delegates, I have never experienced such chaos or such utter disregard for civility, collegiality, and appropriate decorum,” Buckel said. “It has, unfortunately, indelibly marred this session and our good faith efforts to promote civility and collegial behavior on the House floor.”

Peña-Melnyk got out her rule book and responded over the weekend.

“Rule 94 provides members the opportunity to explain their vote when recognized by the Chair — it does not require that explanations be granted in every circumstance, particularly when the House is working against a hard constitutional deadline,” she said in a statement.

Peña-Melnyk said she had extended those courtesies to members “for 89 days, 23 hours and 55 minutes,” and that members had plenty of chances to explain their vote in two hours of debate on the bill just days earlier. But with minutes to midnight and important legislation pending, she said, she “exercised her responsibility to manage the floor and ensure the people’s business was completed. Nothing about that decision violated the rules of the House.”

The conservative Maryland Freedom Caucus, meanwhile, did not bother with a recitation of the rules in a statement it issued the day after Sine Die. It went straight for the legal options to address what it called a “procedurally questionable” maneuver to ram through legislation “over the objections of members of the Maryland Freedom Caucus and the House Republican Caucus.”

“The minority party’s rights and voice were deliberately silenced by the Speaker,” said Del. Kathy Szeliga (D-Baltimore County), in a Freedom Caucus statement. “We are investigating our legal options to defend the minority party’s role in Maryland with all the tools in our toolbox.”

Comptroller Brooke E. Lierman announced this week that Gayon M. Sampson will be her new chief of staff, taking over for Rianna Matthews-Brown, who is set to step down April 30. Sampson is set to begin on June 10.

Sampson has been serving as chief of staff to Frederick Mayor Michael O’Connor, who said Sampson has been an “invaluable resource to me” and to the people of Frederick. Sampson, an eighth-generation resident of Frederick, has “helped lead major initiatives that strengthened the City’s operations, expanded economic opportunity, and enhanced collaboration across all levels of government,” according to a statement from Lierman.
“Gayon is a thoughtful, results-driven leader who understands how to bring people together to get things done,” Lierman said. “His experience in local government and in the business sector, combined with his strong track record of improving operations and delivering results for residents, makes him the right person to help lead our agency forward.”
Before his time as Frederick chief of staff, Sampson was a senior adviser to the Frederick mayor, helping develop the City’s first 10-year strategic plan. He has also worked with Johns Hopkins University and Medicine and the Greater Baltimore Committee, focusing on government relations, policy and community engagement, Lierman’s statement said.
“Public service is about doing the work and delivering for people, and I’m grateful for the opportunity to do that alongside Comptroller Lierman and her team,” Sampson said. “In this role, I will be committed to building strong relationships across the agency and across the state, and ensuring our work earns and maintains the public’s trust.”
Sampson holds a master of public administration from the University of Maryland, College Park, and a bachelor’s degree in political science from Towson University.
